item.text: {"question_id":"4B.10","answer":"The supplied evidence does not establish that López Obrador left political freedom and democratic resilience durably stronger than inherited. Mexico retained meaningful electoral competition, online and civic mobilization, independent outlets, and institutions capable of review: elections were generally free and fair, opposition power alternation remained realistic, the INE continued under prior rules during the Plan B litigation, and the Supreme Court invalidated Plan B for legislative-procedure violations and rejected the transfer of National Guard control to Defense as unconstitutional. These are important resilience and correction mechanisms, but they primarily show inherited or societal and institutional constraints operating against executive initiatives, not ruler-led self-binding. During the period, López Obrador’s administration also pursued reforms and practices that threatened those constraints, including Plan B, pressure and delays affecting autonomous bodies, support for dissolving INAI, expanded military control, pressure on courts and media, and persistent impunity and arbitrary-detention concerns. Positive measures—including strengthened gender-violence laws, refugee-system capacity, UN cooperation, victim-reparation and investigative mechanisms, and some judicially reviewable reforms—were real but mixed in attribution, implementation, durability, and effect. The best-supported conclusion is therefore a mixed trajectory with substantial ruler-attributable institutional erosion, partly offset by resilient independent and societal correctives; the evidence is insufficient to show a durable net strengthening of political freedom through institutions enacted and implemented by the
